doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

chapter: Life and work in New York
title: Declining big band work; Mercer Ellington; core musicians
summary: She left the Mercer Ellington Orchestra after a road trip and works with a rotating core of players.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Have you ever done any of the big band opportunities, or pit work?

No. I did that when I first came to New York and I had a very bad experience, and when I left college I was asked to join the Mercer Ellington Orchestra. I went on some road trip with them to New Jersey. I was still in music school at the time. And I just didn’t think that that was the direction for me. I know that’s a way that many instrumentalists apprentice before they find themselves in the world of jazz, but I followed a different path, I really did. I just didn’t think that that was going to be musically helpful to me at that time. And so I went it alone.
To get your own stuff played, it must be imperative that you have a core of people that you try to work with as much as possible, as we saw at the IAJE.
Yeah, and it changes from time to time too, but yeah a body of musicians who get inside your work.
Is it hard to keep a core of people to provide enough work for them?

Sure. And often you have a number of people, not just one bassist who you work with but several, and likewise rhythm sections, so that you’ve sort of worked on your music intimately with a number of musicians so that you’re not locked into just one or two people. Although when you really want that special feeling there are certain people that do a certain thing a certain way, and no other people can do that, or no other chemistry of a group of people can do it the same way. So you get used to understanding that.
